P1.evidence: No setter, nothing to read back. The frame ran in the same compressed three-part form the rep uses on every call — 'It's just an opportunity for me to understand you, you know, where are you today? Where do you want to be? If we can help, I can kind of show you some options' — covering where you are, where you want to go and options, but omitting what is in the way and what you need. Agreement was sought on time rather than on the frame: 'Brandon, do you have the full 45 to an hour available for the call?' — 'Uh, I do. Yes, sir.' That is a real expectation-set and scores partial, but it is not the scripted 'does that work?'. Open question ran verbatim.

P2.evidence: Weak, and weakest where it mattered most. Age and height were never asked; weight was volunteered ('I'm at around 183, 185'). Health conditions and hereditary history were never asked at all. Injuries were never asked, and the prospect gave the rep an open door he walked straight past — 'I don't have to wake up in pain or be limping or something like that' at 00:04:42 was never followed up. Training week and days actually trained were never established, which is a remarkable omission given this man is a professional fitness instructor teaching Pilates and metabolic training most evenings. Diet was not asked; the prior nutritionist history surfaced by itself at 00:35:00, forty minutes in. Energy was not touched. Sleep gets a partial only because the 5am/9pm arithmetic was worked through in detail, though the prospect drove that himself. The 7-out-of-10-then-versus-4-now scale did useful work on results and is credited as a partial on P2f.

P3.evidence: Excellent. The rep refused the surface answer and kept going: 'Who do you really want to show up as?' produced 'an honest man' and a long unprompted disclosure about saying one thing and doing another. Then 'aside from the vanity, aside from being more shredded... what feeling are you actually striving for?' produced a single word, 'Courage', which is the best piece of discovery in this batch. The ripple ran deliberately — 'How is this going to impact the different arenas of Brandon's life?', followed by 'when you say relationships, you're talking about parents, siblings, girlfriend?' — and reached identity, self-worth and the pattern of settling for less than he wants. P3c is the one clean miss: he was never asked what he physically wants to do and cannot. The reflect-back came as an aphorism rather than the scripted contrast — 'We don't get what we want. We get who we are' — hence partial.

P4.evidence: The gap got named clearly and by the prospect himself, which is what the phase exists for: 'I can have some semblance of a routine if I do it by myself, but the time where I was really consistent was whenever I had some support.' He also diagnosed the root cause unprompted as decision paralysis — 'because of this illusion of choice... it actually paralyzes me and makes me do nothing.' But the rep asked almost none of it. The 2023 trainer, the 2021 nutritionist and the details of what worked were all volunteered. P4f was handled indirectly and rather well when the prospect raised the objection his friends make — 'you literally do training yourself, like, why do you need this?' — which the rep met with 'Did Michael Jordan not have a personal coach? How many coaches does Tom Brady have?'. That is the right instinct but it is not the scripted move.

P5.evidence: The best-run consequence frame in this batch. 'What happens if you don't?' got the honest answer 'I'm just coming back where I am right now'. The settle-for move ran in its strongest form — 'a lot of people are okay just settling. I don't get the impression that's you, but what makes you different?' — and the follow-up produced a long, genuinely useful answer ending 'I just know that I am aimed for better. I only have one life, I only have one spirit.' The line in the sand ran twice: 'So are you actually ready to take that step?' — 'Yes', and later 'Time for a change? Time for a change.' P5a is only partial because the two-year horizon was never drawn out; the question was asked once and the answer accepted without dwelling.

P6.evidence: Run properly and in the right order, which makes this the only call in the batch where phase 6 worked. The alignment check ran before any price — 'ten is, yeah, trust these guys to help me step into who I need to be, and one is, ah, I'm not sure if I need this' — and the answer was unambiguous: 'More so leaning on, like, this is something that I need.' P6a ran as 'do you feel internally capable of actually stepping into Brandon 2.0's shoes?' and got 'It's going to be a scary one, but that's one I gotta do scared.' P6b ran as the money-aside isolation, which is the strongest version of it: 'Money aside, investment aside for a moment, do you actually want to do this?' — 'Oh, absolutely' — 'So as long as we figure out the money part, you're in.' A clear yes existed before the offer. The problem on this call is not phase 6.

P11.evidence: Payment collection was initiated on the record — 'So, I'll put this link in the chat, and I'll walk you through' — and the rep confirmed the email address on file before saying 'I'm going to remove my note taker. Obviously, this is sensitive information that we're about to take.' Everything after that is off the record: whether payment completed, whether the Trevor onboarding call was booked, whether an agreement email was sent and signed on the call, and whether the welcome email, Skool link and onboarding questionnaire were walked through. Those three checks are marked not applicable rather than miss because the absence is a recording decision and not demonstrated failure.

objection_plays.detail: The most complete run of the money play in this batch, and that is precisely the problem. Isolation ran first and cleanly ('Money aside, investment aside for a moment, do you actually want to do this?' then 'So as long as we figure out the money part, you're in'). Permission was sought ('you're open to me asking you a couple of questions on the finances'). Then the financial picture ran essentially in full: cash on hand ($600), credit cards (none — he cannot use any credit line), savings ($1,500-2,000), disposable income after bills ($800-1,000), and investments (Roth IRA $200-300; 401k/401b about $6,000-7,000). By the letter of the playbook this is a hit. What it demonstrates is that the play has no stop condition. The prospect had already stated he is in Chapter 7 bankruptcy proceedings; the script gives the rep no instruction to halt, and the completed financial picture was then used to construct payment options against savings and disposable income he had just said were spoken for. The playbook should be amended to make active insolvency a hard stop before the financial picture runs, not an input to it.

Fear was live and named by the prospect repeatedly — 'I think I live a life in fear, sometimes', 'the fear of failure or the fear of success', and the cold pool image. The PLANE move ran well: 'it's kind of like standing on an airplane ready to skydive when you haven't skydived before. And the longer you look down, guess what feeling grows stronger?'. The responsibility transfer landed ('who's responsible for actually taking that leap off the plane... despite the fear?' — 'me'). But the certainty question was never asked, the pleasure-versus-pain question was never asked, the BRIDGE and BURNED BEFORE moves never ran, and the rep started the FEAR acronym and abandoned it mid-sentence: 'it's an acronym for it, but it's not really coming to my mind at the moment'. Started and partly abandoned.
He never asked for time to think; his hesitation was purely arithmetic.
Recently single; no third-party approval gate raised.
Timing was never the objection. He wanted to start; he could not pay.

A script gap that should be added to the known list and treated as the highest priority of the three: the genuinely insolvent prospect. This is not the OC scenario of a capable payer who needs to be shown how. He is in active Chapter 7 proceedings, has no credit access, and calculated live that any instalment puts him in the negative. The playbook contains no disqualification path, no language for ending the call, and no threshold below which the rep is required to stop selling. In the absence of one, the rep improvised downward through four price points and closed a man who said 'No, I can't do that' and 'Yeah, I can't do this' and who described himself as bummed out and broken thirty seconds after agreeing. Every other rep facing this will improvise too until the script tells them what to do.

Second unscripted trigger: the employer-provided free alternative. At 00:00:43 the prospect said of the gym he is joining, 'obviously that particular gym, they would give me training for it'. His employer will teach him kettlebells at no cost. This was never engaged with at any point in fifty-nine minutes. It is a variant of the cheaper-alternative gap already on the known list, but sharper — the substitute is free, credentialled and already committed.

notes: Phases 3, 5 and 6 were run well and in the right order — this is the rep's best process work in the batch and 'Courage' is a genuinely excellent piece of discovery. That makes the ending harder to look at, not easier: a well-qualified emotional yes was converted into a sale to a man in bankruptcy proceedings by walking the price from $4,000 to $1,500 x3 to $2,000 x2 to $1,200 after two explicit refusals. Two things follow. For the rep: the baseline phase is nearly absent across every call and needs drilling. For the business: this is not a coaching problem. The OC play ran to completion exactly as written and produced this outcome, so the fix is a stop condition in the playbook and a control on off-menu pricing, not more training.
